headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 6 studies yielded an effect size of 1.15 (95% CI: 0.94–1.41), indicating no statistically significant association between processed meat intake and renal cell carcinoma. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 77.10%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

studies.Reference: Fat, protein, and meat consumption and renal cell cancer risk: a pooled analysis of 13 prospective studies.
studies.Title: Fat, protein, and meat consumption and renal cell cancer risk: a pooled analysis of 13 prospective studies.
studies.Authors: Lee JE, Spiegelman D, Hunter DJ, Albanes D, Bernstein L, van den Brandt PA, Buring JE, Cho E, English DR, Freudenheim JL, Giles GG, Graham S, Horn-Ross PL, Håkansson N, Leitzmann MF, Männistö S, McCullough ML, Miller AB, Parker AS, Rohan TE, Schatzkin A, Schouten LJ, Sweeney C, Willett WC, Wolk A, Zhang SM, Smith-Warner SA
studies.Journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
studies.Population: Pooling Project of Prospective Studies of Diet and Cancer cohorts

cases.excerpt: A total of 1478 incident cases of renal cell cancer were identified (709 in women and 769 in men).

effect_size.excerpt: The pooled corrected RRs for a 5% increment of energy intake from monounsaturated fat was 1.32 (95% CI = 1.02 to 1.69) and from total protein was 1.21 (95% CI = 0.93 to 1.58), which were slightly higher than the respective pooled uncorrected adjusted RRs (RR for 5% increment of energy intake from monounsaturated fat = 1.15; 95% CI = 1.04 to 1.27 and RR for 5% increment of energy intake from total protein = 1.08; 95% CI = 0.99 to 1.19). Intakes of red meat, processed meat, poultry, and seafood were not associated with the risk of renal cell cancer regardless of whether RRs were estimated by the categorical ( Table 4 ), continuous ( Table 4 ), or quartile (data not shown) models.

confidence_interval.excerpt: For example, in the analyses of total fat, the pooled age-adjusted RR of renal cell cancer for the highest vs the lowest quintile of intake—1.30 (95% CI = 1.08 to 1.56)—was attenuated to 1.23 (95% CI = 1.03 to 1.46) after adjusting for BMI, to 1.25 (95% CI = 1.06 to 1.48) after adjusting for alcohol intake, and to 1.24 (95% CI = 1.02 to 1.51) after adjusting for fruit and vegetable intake.

p_value.excerpt: For example, the pooled multivariable RR for the highest vs the lowest quintile of total fat intake was 1.10 (95% CI = 0.92 to 1.32; P trend = .31).

design.excerpt: We conducted a pooled analysis of 13 prospective studies

timing.excerpt: and had follow-up times of up to 7–20 years to examine associations between meat, fat, and protein intakes and the risk of renal cell cancer.

ethnicity.excerpt: The Pooling Project of Prospective Studies of Diet and Cancer (referred to hereafter as the Pooling Project) is an international consortium of cohort studies whose goal is to analyze diet and cancer associations ( 19 ).

exposure_measurement.excerpt: The processed meat group included sausage, bacon, hot dog, ham, and luncheon meat.

studies.Authors: Ziouziou I, Shariat SF, Ajdi F, Khabbal Y
studies.Population: 170 countries with available data on age-standardized incidence and mortality rates of RCC and dietary factors
studies.comparison_type: per-unit increase in country-level processed meat intake (multivariable linear regression on age-standardized RCC incidence rate)

sample_size.excerpt: We conducted an ecological study including 170 countries, whose data on age-standardized (AS) incidence and mortality rates of RCC, dietary factors, and potentially confounding factors such as obesity, insufficient physical activity, tobacco smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and human development index (HDI) were collected and available on May 2020 from the Global Cancer Observatory, the Global Dietary Database, the Global Health Observatory data repository, the Diabetes Atlas 9th edition and the Human Development Report 2019.

effect_size.excerpt: Intake of processed meats and consumption of alcohol were both positively associated with AS incidence rates of RCC (β = 0.11, P < 0.001 and β = 0.1, P = 0.044, respectively). We suggest that high consumption of processed meats and/or alcohol is a risk factor for RCC.
